power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: Our estimated effect size was drawn from a similar study that found small-moderate effects of teacher training on student engagement (d ≈ 0.4) [23]. We used data from our preliminary work to get other parameters for sample size estimation: 5 teachers per school; 16 student responses per teacher; 2% of variance accounted for by school; 5.5% of variance accounted for by class. We used PANGEA (v0.2) [38] to calculate power for our design.

Given the above parameters, we needed 9 schools in each of the treatment and control groups to reach >80% power. To account for 10% school drop-out, we aimed for 20 low-SES schools to be randomised and 10 high-SES comparison schools.

text.text: This version corrects the earlier one.

We audited the data and analysis code behind the earlier version, including every analysed student's link to their teacher, and corrected the following: 1.40 students who named a waitlist teacher had been given an intervention teacher's code and analysed as intervention.
The engagement and agentic engagement effects reported in the earlier version came from this error.
2.55 intervention-arm students whose teachers consented but did not start, or stopped, the training had been excluded.
They are now analysed as allocated (intention to treat), as the protocol specifies.
3.33 students who named a teacher who had not consented had been matched by hand to a consenting teacher.
They are now excluded, by the same rule as other students of non-consenting teachers.
4.4 students of two consenting teachers whose consent had been misrecorded are now included.

5.64 students had submitted the follow-up survey twice and were counted twice; each is now analysed once. 10 students whose follow-up had been linked to another student's baseline are analysed without a baseline.
The mathematics mindset items had been scored in the opposite direction to the PE items, and three mathematics goal subscales used the PE item order (these did not enter the effect estimates).
Physical activity is now reported in days; the earlier means were response codes, one higher.
7.12 mathematics students who had named teachers of PE are now excluded, as other students who named a teacher of the other subject already were.
Country of birth and home language now follow students' typed answers where these disagreed with the tick-box.
The analysis now uses the pre-registered analysis of covariance (follow-up adjusted for baseline) with random intercepts for schools and teachers, tested with Satterthwaite t tests.
The earlier long-format model did not account for clustering of the intervention effect within schools and teachers, so its confidence intervals were too narrow.
Corrected sample: 1,877 students in 27 schools.

The intervention did not improve engagement in any specification (full sample: d = 0.01, 95% CI [-0.14, 0.16]; P = 0.890, P_FDR = 0.933), and no outcome differed after correction for multiple comparisons.

Among students who completed baseline by the end of Week 1 of Year 7, estimates for physical activity (d = 0.24, 95% CI [0.04, 0.43]; P = 0.019, P_FDR = 0.521) and need satisfaction (d = 0.19, 95% CI [-0.01, 0.38]; P = 0.063, P_FDR = 0.551) favoured the intervention, but neither was significant after correction (need satisfaction was not significant even before it); in the full sample both were smaller (physical activity (d = 0.10, 95% CI [-0.09, 0.28]; P = 0.265, P_FDR = 0.879); need satisfaction (d = 0.02, 95% CI [-0.20, 0.25]; P = 0.841, P_FDR = 0.904)).

The text was also shortened and restructured, and it now reports three measures the earlier version left out: the pre-registered teacher manipulation check, students' ratings of the targeted teacher behaviours, and the relative autonomy index.
The corrected data and code, with each correction documented in code/data_corrections.R, are on the OSF project (https://osf.io/m7rb9/).
text.formatted: The corrected data and code, with each correction documented in code/data_corrections.R, are on the OSF project (<ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/m7rb9/">https://osf.io/m7rb9/</ref>).

text.text: In their first nine years of school, students spend 7,533 hours being taught [1], and teachers are among the most influential factors for outcomes [2].
text.formatted: In their first nine years of school, students spend 7,533 hours being taught <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref>, and teachers are among the most influential factors for outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref>.

text.text: Most research on teacher effects has focused on achievement.
Here we examine how teacher behaviour influences student engagement, a prerequisite for successful learning [3].
text.formatted: Here we examine how teacher behaviour influences student engagement, a prerequisite for successful learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref>.

text.text: Engagement refers to how students think (cognitive engagement), feel (emotional engagement), and what they do to make progress (behavioural engagement) [4].
text.formatted: Engagement refers to how students think (cognitive engagement), feel (emotional engagement), and what they do to make progress (behavioural engagement) <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref>.

text.text: Less engaged students are more likely to be disruptive, struggle academically and drop out [5].
text.formatted: Less engaged students are more likely to be disruptive, struggle academically and drop out <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref>.

text.text: School engagement predicts academic performance [6] and even occupational attainment around 20 years later [7].
text.formatted: School engagement predicts academic performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref> and even occupational attainment around 20 years later <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref>.

text.text: Teacher behaviours can nourish or stifle engagement [8], so helping teachers adopt nourishing behaviours is a logical strategy.
text.formatted: Teacher behaviours can nourish or stifle engagement <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref>, so helping teachers adopt nourishing behaviours is a logical strategy.

text.text: It may also be cost-effective and scalable, because each teacher works with dozens of students, often for years.
Like achievement, engagement is domain-specific [9, 10].
text.formatted: Like achievement, engagement is domain-specific <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10]</ref>.

text.text: A student can be highly engaged in physical education (PE) yet disengaged in mathematics.
We studied mathematics and PE because engagement in both declines during the transition to secondary school and because they are contrasting instructional environments.
Mathematics emphasises abstract reasoning and individual problem-solving; PE involves embodied learning, teamwork and public performance.
The teacher behaviours that matter may therefore differ between subjects, so we designed a separate intervention for each.
A targeted approach to increasing engagement Performance in both mathematics and PE is declining in Australia.
PISA mathematics scores have fallen faster than reading or science scores, and further than the OECD average [11].
text.formatted: PISA mathematics scores have fallen faster than reading or science scores, and further than the OECD average <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref>.

text.text: Australia received a D-for physical fitness on its most recent Physical Activity Report Card [12].
text.formatted: Australia received a D-for physical fitness on its most recent Physical Activity Report Card <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref>.

text.text: In both subjects students learn by doing: in mathematics by attempting problems, asking questions and discussing ideas [13], and in PE by running, jumping and throwing rather than sitting and listening [14].
text.formatted: In both subjects students learn by doing: in mathematics by attempting problems, asking questions and discussing ideas <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref>, and in PE by running, jumping and throwing rather than sitting and listening <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref>.

text.text: Engaging students is therefore central to learning in both.
Children from disadvantaged backgrounds are more likely to become disengaged [4].
text.formatted: Children from disadvantaged backgrounds are more likely to become disengaged <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref>.

text.text: With fewer supports at home and school, they may benefit more from interventions [15].
text.formatted: With fewer supports at home and school, they may benefit more from interventions <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref>.

text.text: A meta-analysis of 101 interventions for students of low socioeconomic status (SES) found that they improved learning, particularly in mathematics, but not by enough to close the gap explained by socioeconomic advantage [16].
text.formatted: A meta-analysis of 101 interventions for students of low socioeconomic status (SES) found that they improved learning, particularly in mathematics, but not by enough to close the gap explained by socioeconomic advantage <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref>.

text.text: We therefore focused on improving engagement in low-SES schools.
We also focused on the transition to secondary school (Year 6 to Year 7 in Australia), "one of the most stressful events in a young person's life" [17].
text.formatted: We also focused on the transition to secondary school (Year 6 to Year 7 in Australia), "one of the most stressful events in a young person's life" <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref>.

text.text: Students lose familiar teachers, routines and friendship groups, and engagement usually drops sharply [18].
text.formatted: Students lose familiar teachers, routines and friendship groups, and engagement usually drops sharply <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18]</ref>.

text.text: Whether engagement drops seems to depend on what teachers do [19].
text.formatted: Whether engagement drops seems to depend on what teachers do <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref>.

text.text: According to self-determination theory [20], teacher behaviours shape students' satisfaction of three basic psychological needs: autonomy (feeling volitional), competence (feeling effective) and relatedness (feeling connected to others).
text.formatted: According to self-determination theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref>, teacher behaviours shape students' satisfaction of three basic psychological needs: autonomy (feeling volitional), competence (feeling effective) and relatedness (feeling connected to others).

text.text: Variety has been proposed as an additional need that may matter most when other needs are poorly satisfied [21].
text.formatted: Variety has been proposed as an additional need that may matter most when other needs are poorly satisfied <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[21]</ref>.

text.text: Teachers satisfy these needs when they offer choice and rationales, set optimal challenges with scaffolding, and show warmth [8, 22].
text.formatted: Teachers satisfy these needs when they offer choice and rationales, set optimal challenges with scaffolding, and show warmth <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">22]</ref>.

text.text: Many trials show that training teachers in need-supportive behaviours can improve student outcomes.

Cheon, Reeve and colleagues have reported consistent effects on motivation, engagement and well-being, mostly in PE [23] [24] [25]; a meta-analysis of selfdetermination theory interventions in education found reliable effects on need satisfaction and autonomous motivation [22]; and web-based autonomy-supportive training can change teacher practice and student experience [26, 27].
text.formatted: Cheon, Reeve and colleagues have reported consistent effects on motivation, engagement and well-being, mostly in PE <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[23]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[24]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[25]</ref>; a meta-analysis of selfdetermination theory interventions in education found reliable effects on need satisfaction and autonomous motivation <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[22]</ref>; and web-based autonomy-supportive training can change teacher practice and student experience <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">[26,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">27]</ref>.

text.text: These interventions share a design feature: researchers or experts select the targets, usually from within self-determination theory [28].
text.formatted: These interventions share a design feature: researchers or experts select the targets, usually from within self-determination theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[28]</ref>.

text.text: However, other theoretical models explain teachers' effects on engagement.
Good teachers act as positive role models (transformational leadership theory [29]), foster growth-oriented beliefs about ability [30] and mastery-focused achievement goals [31].
text.formatted: Good teachers act as positive role models (transformational leadership theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">[29]</ref>), foster growth-oriented beliefs about ability <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">[30]</ref> and mastery-focused achievement goals <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">[31]</ref>.

text.text: Instead of only choosing intervention components based on theory or expert judgement, we chose intervention components empirically [32].
text.formatted: Instead of only choosing intervention components based on theory or expert judgement, we chose intervention components empirically <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">[32]</ref>.

text.text: We used data-driven selection to complement expert judgement.

In an earlier two-wave study of 1,799 Year 7 students in 17 low-SES schools, students rated their teachers on 71 behaviours drawn from four motivational theories, and we used elastic net regression to identify the behaviours that best predicted change in engagement (the PE analyses are published [19]; the mathematics analyses are unpublished).
text.formatted: In an earlier two-wave study of 1,799 Year 7 students in 17 low-SES schools, students rated their teachers on 71 behaviours drawn from four motivational theories, and we used elastic net regression to identify the behaviours that best predicted change in engagement (the PE analyses are published <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref>; the mathematics analyses are unpublished).

text.text: The predictors differed by subject.

In PE, transformational leadership behaviours (e.g., being a good role model) and variety mattered most, consistent with research showing that PE engagement depends on teacher enthusiasm and varied activities [33].
text.formatted: In PE, transformational leadership behaviours (e.g., being a good role model) and variety mattered most, consistent with research showing that PE engagement depends on teacher enthusiasm and varied activities <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">[33]</ref>.

text.text: Our primary hypothesis was that the program would increase student engagement relative to a waitlist control.

We also hypothesised that it would increase psychological need satisfaction, the mechanism proposed by self-determination theory [8, 22]; foster mastery-oriented rather than ego-oriented achievement goals [31, 34]; improve PE students' attitudes toward physical activity through role modelling and variety [35, 36]; increase mathematics students' instrumental motivation, the perceived usefulness of mathematics [37]; and improve physical activity and mathematics achievement as distal outcomes [6, 14].

text.text: We report how we determined our sample size, all data exclusions, all manipulations, and all measures in the study.
We report the trial following the CONSORT 2010 statement and its extension to cluster randomised trials (completed checklist provided as a supplementary file).
Low-SES schools were randomised by school (1:1) to the intervention or waitlist control.
We randomised schools rather than teachers because teachers completed the program in small groups with colleagues from their school, so randomising within schools would have risked contamination.
High-SES schools were waitlisted and analysed as a comparison to see if the intervention could bridge the gap between low-and high-SES schools.

text.text: As shown, baseline data collection occurred directly before the state-wide implementation of COVID-19 lockdowns and remote learning.

The project proceeded largely as pre-registered, but this timing context is important when interpreting results. (workshops from September 2019, with most online module completions by March 2020, a few continuing to December 2020 and one in April 2021); student baseline sessions in Year 6 (November-December 2019) and early Year 7 (29 January-5 March 2020); COVID-19 learning from home in New South Wales (23 March-25 May 2020); teacher follow-up surveys (sent from 28 September 2020) and student follow-up (13 October-8 December 2020); and the program offered to waitlist and comparison schools after follow-up (workshops in November 2020).
One important change to the protocol was made following pre-registration.
We had planned to collect all baseline data before students began Year 7 (e.g., by doing data collection during the school's orientation day).
This schedule aimed to ensure student ratings were uncontaminated by their initial experiences of the Year 7 teacher.
However, the schedule was difficult to achieve because data collection did not fit during some orientation days, and because many students did not attend orientations.

As a result, only 40.3% of analysed students completed baseline in Year 6; the rest completed it during the first three school days of Year 7 (29-31 January 2020) or later in Term 1, up to 5 March 2020.

Timing differed by group: 62.3% of waitlist, 50.5% of comparison and 12.3% of intervention students completed baseline in Year 6, and 98.3%, 72.6% and 30.6%, respectively, did so by the end of Week 1.
As described under Statistical methods, we addressed this with a multiverse analysis that included specifications restricted by baseline timing.

text.text: In that study, we created a taxonomy of 71 teacher behaviours drawn from four major motivational theories: selfdetermination theory, achievement goal theory, growth mindset theory, and transformational leadership theory.
This taxonomy was created by drawing behaviours from questionnaire items in previous research.
From 111 papers, we sourced 49 unique scales, containing 1,151 candidate items.
Each of the 1,151 items was reviewed by two authors and grouped into 'bins' of items measuring similar constructs (e.g., all items measuring 'provides meaningful choices').
If items did not fit any category, a new category was created.
We then had two authors choose the exemplar item that best represented the category; exemplars were member-checked by eight experts in motivation and five teachers from local secondary schools.
This resulted in a list of 71 motivational behaviours.
Students rated their teacher on all 71 behaviours in the middle of a school year, and we tested which behaviours predicted change in engagement across the year.
To manage risks of multicollinearity, we used elastic net regression on the longitudinal data to identify which behaviours best predicted changes in student engagement across the school year.
The six behaviours selected for each subject were those with the strongest predictive validity (R² = 5.09% for total engagement; R² = 4.36% on new data not used in original model fitting).
These proportions of explained variance are consistent with the generally small effects of individual teaching behaviours on student outcomes [42].

text.text: The intervention involved approximately 12 hours of blended teacher professional learning: a 1-hour introductory workshop, usually delivered face to face at the school, followed by approximately 11 hours of online learning and mentoring (the dose registered with the NSW Education Standards Authority).
After the workshop, teachers completed six online, asynchronous modules (1-2 hours per module).
Each module covered one of the six key behaviours identified in the longitudinal data for their subject (Supplementary Table S1).
text.formatted: Each module covered one of the six key behaviours identified in the longitudinal data for their subject (Supplementary Table <ref type="table">S1</ref>).

text.text: Professional learning modules included videos covering each core concept, multiplechoice questions to check teacher understanding, case studies with feedback to apply the concepts, worksheets to apply the concepts to their own teaching, and action plans with examples to put the key behaviours into practice.
Teachers were asked to complete worksheets and modules in small groups with their colleagues, ideally at fortnightly intervals to promote spaced learning and implementation.

Following the six online modules, teachers completed a 1-hour, synchronous online mentoring session to consolidate learning, construct ongoing action plans, and provide accountability for completing the other content.
A detailed curriculum is available on the Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/m7rb9/).

We calculated students' scores by averaging the three engagement subscales (affective, behavioural, and cognitive), consistent with the theoretical model of engagement as a higher-order construct encompassing these dimensions [43].

text.text: Student engagement was designated as the primary outcome because it was the direct target of the intervention.

The protocol listed need satisfaction, which reflects the hypothesised mechanism, as a secondary outcome, together with physical activity, attitudes toward physical activity, achievement goals, mathematics achievement and instrumental motivation.

Agentic engagement was not listed in either version of the protocol, and mindset beliefs and the relative autonomy index were listed in the original version but removed in the 12 November 2019 update, before student data collection; we collected all three and report them as exploratory outcomes.
We assessed a range of theory-driven antecedents and outcomes of engagement.
We received ethics approval for these measures before finalising the specific intervention components.
Thus, the secondary outcomes are not matched to intervention components; they test the intervention's possible mechanisms.

text.text: We computed a relative autonomy index by weighting these reasons +3, +2, +1, -1, -2 and -3, respectively, and averaging.
We measured teacher completion of the online learning using the analytics from our learning management system.
These analytics reported each individual teacher's completion of each step of each module (e.g., whether they completed the multiple-choice questions or submitted an open-ended question).
We operationalised 'completion' as having done at least 95% of the course.
As pre-registered, we also assessed teachers' beliefs about the target behaviours.
At baseline and follow-up, teachers rated how effective each of the six target behaviours for their subject is for developing student motivation, on a 10-point scale.

We reverse-scored the two behaviours the program taught teachers to avoid (unfair rewards in PE and harsh critical language in mathematics), averaged the six ratings, and compared intervention and waitlist teachers' standardised follow-up scores using linear regression adjusted for baseline scores.
A random intercept for schools was estimated at zero, so we report the single-level model.
As a student-reported fidelity check, students rated at follow-up how much their teacher displayed each of the six target behaviours for their subject, on a 7-point scale.
We reverse-scored the behaviour the program taught teachers to avoid, averaged the six ratings, and analysed this score in the same multiverse as the outcomes.
Following registration, we had a hypothesis that teachers would be less engaged in the intervention if they perceived the core behaviours were 'common sense'.
As an exploratory analysis, we asked teachers how confident they were in each of the six behaviours before starting the intervention.
They responded on a 10-point scale from 'not at all confident' to 'extremely confident'.
We used a Euclidean distance minimisation strategy to create pairs of similar low-SES schools for randomisation.

The schools were matched on: (i) ICSEA, (ii) school size (number of students enrolled), (iii) public results from the national standardised tests of numeracy and literacy, which are completed by all New South Wales children.
Following baseline data collection of the teacher outcomes, low-SES schools were paired on those variables then randomly assigned to the experimental or control arm.
An experienced statistician who was not part of the research team used a computer-generated algorithm to conduct the randomisation procedure.
Students were blind to the experimental manipulation.
We were unable to keep teachers blinded to conditions because they were aware of the training during recruitment for the trial.
We could not prevent teachers from discussing the training with students, but believed the likelihood of this influencing results would be low.

As pre-registered, we analysed each outcome measured at baseline and follow-up with a linear mixed model (restricted maximum likelihood) of the follow-up score, with condition (intervention, waitlist, high-SES comparison) and the baseline score as fixed effects, and subject (mathematics vs.
PE) as a covariate when both subjects were analysed together.

Random intercepts for schools and for teachers nested within schools accounted for clustering; the protocol specified students nested within teachers, and we added the school level because schools were the unit of randomisation.

Mindset beliefs, the relative autonomy index and student-rated teacher behaviours were measured only at follow-up, so those models omitted the baseline score; because mindset beliefs were rated on different scales in the two subjects, we standardised them within subject before pooling.

We analysed students according to their school's randomised allocation regardless of how much of the program their teacher completed, including students of teachers who never started it (intention to treat; the per-protocol analysis is the exception).
For model parsimony we did not test random slopes.

Because students were linked to teachers only at follow-up, the analysed sample comprises students who completed follow-up and could be matched to a participating teacher; students who left before follow-up cannot be identified, so we could not assess attrition between baseline and follow-up, or use the full-information maximum likelihood planned in the protocol.
The eight intervention and waitlist students (0.6%) without a baseline score were excluded from models that adjusted for baseline.

text.text: We report each intervention effect as the standardised mean difference between intervention and waitlist students in the follow-up score, adjusted for baseline where measured (Cohen's d in total-standard-deviation units of the outcome).

We tested each effect with a two-tailed t test using Satterthwaite degrees of freedom [52], which allows for the small number of schools and teachers per arm, and report 95% confidence intervals from the same t distribution.

text.text: In our case, for each outcome, we presented the results using three subsets of the data, then additional specifications described below.
As mentioned earlier, we had hoped to collect all data before students entered Year 7, so we presented results using only these data (40.3% of students, but only 12.3% of intervention students).
We also present results for the full sample, including students who completed baseline data collection up to six weeks into Year 7.
This may not be a valid baseline because students had experience with their Year 7 teacher, who was already implementing the strategies of the intervention.

As a compromise between having an adequate sample size and a valid baseline, we also present results for students who completed baseline before the end of Week 1 of Year 7 (65.9% of students; 30.6% of intervention students).

The first three school days of Year 7 (29-31 January 2020) would be unlikely to contaminate student responses, but including these students increases our sample size, especially for the intervention group.

As per our pre-registered analysis plan, we also conducted analyses that controlled for student demographic characteristics (gender, self-reported wealth on a social status ladder, the number of books reported in the home, language at home, and country of birth).
For these models involving covariates, we used the data for students who completed baseline before the end of Week 1 of Year 7.

We also pre-registered a per-protocol analysis restricted to intervention teachers who completed more than 90% of the program (24 of 40 intervention teachers); in the Week 1 subsample, where we ran it, the same teachers would be selected at a 95% threshold.
Finally, we estimated effects separately for PE and mathematics students and, for need satisfaction, with and without variety.
By using a multiverse analysis, we can see whether the intervention effects are sensitive to these analytical decisions.
We used Claude (Anthropic) to check the data and analysis code for errors, to fix any errors it identified, and to help edit the text.
The authors reviewed all changes and take full responsibility for the content.
Effects on psychological need satisfaction Need satisfaction did not differ reliably between intervention and waitlist students.

Of the three samples, the estimate was largest among students who completed baseline by the end of Week 1 (d = 0.19, 95% CI [-0.01, 0.38]; P = 0.063, P FDR = 0.551); in this subsample, need satisfaction fell less among intervention students than the other groups (Fig 4B).

The estimate was larger for PE students (d = 0.25, 95% CI [0.02, 0.47]; P = 0.034, P FDR = 0.521) than for mathematics students (d = 0.10, 95% CI [-0.39, 0.60]; P = 0.626, P FDR = 0.899), but no estimate survived FDR correction, and this subsample's intervention arm comprised 214 students of 16 teachers in 4 schools (81% in two of them).
Estimates were close to zero in the full sample (d = 0.02, 95% CI [-0.20, 0.25]; P = 0.841, P FDR = 0.904) and the Year 6 subsample (d = 0.04, 95% CI [-0.24, 0.32]; P = 0.783, P FDR = 0.899).

Within the Week 1 subsample, the estimate was similar without variety (d = 0.17, 95% CI [-0.04, 0.38]; P = 0.102, P FDR = 0.665) and in the per-protocol analysis (d = 0.20, 95% CI [-0.06, 0.46]; P = 0.128, P FDR = 0.665), which included 104 intervention students of 7 teachers. respectively).
None of the remaining secondary or exploratory outcomes showed effects that survived FDR correction (Supplementary Fig. S2).
text.formatted: None of the remaining secondary or exploratory outcomes showed effects that survived FDR correction (Supplementary Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">S2</ref>).

text.text: In the full sample, there were no effects on achievement goal orientations, including self-approach goals (d = -0.04, 95% CI [-0.31, 0.23]; P = 0.746, P FDR = 0.899), self-avoidance goals (d = 0.06, 95% CI [-0.14, 0.26]; P = 0.533, P FDR = 0.899), other-approach goals (d = -0.05, 95% CI [-0.29, 0.19]; P = 0.667, P FDR = 0.899), or other-avoidance goals (d = -0.07, 95% CI [-0.31, 0.18]; P = 0.574, P FDR = 0.899).

Similarly, there were no effects on students' attitude toward physical activity (d = 0.05, 95% CI [-0.12, 0.21]; P = 0.556, P FDR = 0.899), their instrumental motivation for mathematics (d = -0.03, 95% CI [-0.28, 0.22]; P = 0.807, P FDR = 0.899), their mathematics achievement (d = 0.06, 95% CI [-0.33, 0.44]; P = 0.744, P FDR = 0.899), or PE students' relative autonomy for attending school (d = 0.16, 95% CI [-0.18, 0.50]; P = 0.336, P FDR = 0.879).

Nor were there effects on mindset beliefs in the full sample, either incremental (d = 0.03, 95% CI [-0.30, 0.37]; P = 0.846, P FDR = 0.904) or entity beliefs (d = -0.02, 95% CI [-0.19, 0.14]; P = 0.753, P FDR = 0.899).

In the subsamples, intervention students reported weaker entity beliefs in the Week 1 subsample (d = -0.19, 95% CI [-0.38, -0.01]; P = 0.044, P FDR = 0.521) and weaker incremental beliefs in the Year 6 subsample (d = -0.50, 95% CI [-0.96, -0.05]; P = 0.032, P FDR = 0.521), whose intervention students attended 3 schools; neither survived FDR correction (Supplementary Fig. S2).

text.text: Implementation was bimodal.
Of the 40 intervention teachers whose students were analysed, 23 (58%) completed at least 95% of the program, while 10 (25%) completed less than 10%.

The learning management system recorded the introductory workshop as complete for 34 of these teachers (85%): 30 in September-November 2019, before the COVID-19 pandemic, 2 early in 2020 and 2 later in 2020; 1 completed part of it and 5 did not start it.
The system did not record whether each teacher attended face to face or online.

Of the 504 course activities (workshops, modules, worksheets and reflections) recorded as complete for these teachers, 73% occurred before April 2020, 25% between April 2020 and the start of student follow-up, and 2% after follow-up had begun.

Teachers reported high confidence in the target behaviours before the program (M = 8.32/10, SD = 1.04; n = 25 teachers with ratings), but prior confidence was not reliably associated with completion (r = -0.19, P = 0.356, n = 25).

At follow-up, intervention teachers rated the target behaviours as slightly more effective than waitlist teachers did, adjusting for baseline ratings, but the difference was not significant (d = 0.21, 95% CI [-0.10, 0.52]; P = 0.177).
This analysis included all teachers with ratings at both time points (36 intervention and 53 waitlist teachers), of whom 25 and 30, respectively, taught students in the analysed sample.

Students' ratings of their teacher on the six target behaviours at follow-up did not differ between intervention and waitlist teachers in any specification, including the full sample (d = -0.04, 95% CI [-0.35, 0.28]; P = 0.806, P FDR = 0.899) and the Week 1 subsample (d = 0.15, 95% CI [-0.22, 0.53]; P = 0.419, P FDR = 0.899; Supplementary Fig. S2).

text.text: We therefore have no evidence that teachers changed the targeted behaviours; we return to this limitation in the Discussion.
This study tested whether a data-informed approach to selecting intervention targets could improve student engagement during the transition to secondary school.
The intervention did not improve engagement, the primary outcome, in any specification, and no secondary or exploratory outcome differed after correction for multiple comparisons.

Among students who completed baseline by the end of Week 1, estimates for physical activity and need satisfaction favoured the intervention, but neither was significant after correction (need satisfaction was not significant even before it), and both rest on an intervention arm from only 4 schools, so they are hypotheses to test rather than effects.

Students did not report that intervention teachers used the targeted behaviours more, and teachers' beliefs about those behaviours did not change reliably, so we have no evidence that the program changed teaching.
Our teacher data suggest one reason for the weak effects.

Before the program, teachers were already very confident in the target behaviours (M = 8.32/10), and some suggestions may have seemed obvious (e.g., 'use variety' in PE; 'use fair discipline' in mathematics).

Yet in our longitudinal data, students reported that some teachers displayed these behaviours far more than others, and the difference mattered to them [19]; teachers' views of their own behaviour often differ from students' views [55].

text.text: Confident teachers may not see a personal need for training, and perceived usefulness predicts engagement in professional learning [56], although prior confidence was not reliably associated with completion here.

text.text: Personalised feedback, such as lesson observations or feedback on video [57], may be needed to change behaviours that teachers regard as common sense.

text.text: The COVID-19 pandemic also added to teachers' workload at a stressful time and may have reduced their engagement with the program.

Our estimates were smaller than those of the Cheon and Reeve program, which has produced consistently positive effects on motivation in PE through more intensive face-toface training and coaching [25].
text.formatted: Our estimates were smaller than those of the Cheon and Reeve program, which has produced consistently positive effects on motivation in PE through more intensive face-toface training and coaching <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[25]</ref>.

text.text: Paap and colleagues [27] tested a web-based need-supportive program for PE teachers and found small effects on physical activity, which suggests that delivery format, rather than how targets are selected, may limit effect sizes.

text.text: The physical activity estimates would be important if replicated, but we treat them with caution.

They did not survive correction for multiple comparisons, they were smaller in the full sample, and intervention students reported less physical activity than students in the other groups at baseline.
Physical activity was also self-reported with a single item, which is less valid than device-based measures.
Future studies of interventions like ours should measure physical activity with accelerometers or similar devices.
Other secondary outcomes were weak tests of the program.
We registered outcomes before using data to choose the intervention components, so several were not matched to those components.
For example, no mathematics component addressed career relevance, so the null effect on instrumental motivation is unsurprising.

Behaviours that predict engagement need not influence every motivational outcome; targeting career value would require behaviours such as connecting mathematics to future study and work, which were not top predictors in our data.
Several other limitations constrain interpretation.

First, we did not observe classroom practice, and neither the pre-registered manipulation check (teachers' beliefs about the effectiveness of the target behaviours) nor students' ratings of the targeted behaviours showed reliable change, so we cannot confirm that teachers changed their behaviour.
Engagement was self-reported across a whole term, whereas some trials with large effects used blind observer ratings [58].
text.formatted: Engagement was self-reported across a whole term, whereas some trials with large effects used blind observer ratings <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">[58]</ref>.

text.text: Future trials should observe teaching, in person or by video.

Second, only 12.3% of intervention students completed baseline before Year 7, and restricting by baseline timing left few intervention clusters (4 schools in the Week 1 subsample and 3 in the Year 6 subsample), so those estimates are fragile.

Third, two intervention schools withdrew and a third stopped the training, so 8 intervention schools were analysed, fewer than the 9 per arm assumed in our power calculation, and fewer still received the program as intended.

Collecting baseline data before students met their Year 7 teachers proved difficult, and we surveyed many students who were not taught by participating teachers; asking Year 7 teachers to run the baseline survey in their first lesson would avoid both problems, at the cost of extra teacher workload.
Fourth, the earlier study explained about 5% of the variance in engagement, a modest basis for selecting targets.
Fifth, the light-touch online format likely reduced completion.

Engagement in professional learning depends on time, support and interaction [56]; we recommend first testing a prototype with more support and then adapting it for scale, because a program designed for scale from the start offers few chances to iterate in response to user feedback.
text.formatted: Engagement in professional learning depends on time, support and interaction <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">[56]</ref>; we recommend first testing a prototype with more support and then adapting it for scale, because a program designed for scale from the start offers few chances to iterate in response to user feedback.

text.text: Finally, we compared the program with a waitlist rather than with an intervention whose components were chosen by expert judgement, which is the comparison needed to test data-informed selection itself.
The research team comprised university-based academics who were not members of the low-SES communities where the research took place.
We designed the intervention with teachers but did not involve students or families.
Student-reported data drove target selection, which partly offsets researcher assumptions, but future work should centre the perspectives of students and families in these communities.
This study tested a model for building targeted interventions to support students, especially those from lower socioeconomic backgrounds, during one of their most difficult transitions.
Using data to identify the teacher behaviours that best predicted engagement, we built a brief, mostly online professional learning program and delivered it during a disrupted year.
It did not improve engagement.

The physical activity and need satisfaction estimates that favoured the intervention could be tested in larger trials with more schools per arm, direct observation of teaching, and device-based measures of activity.

For practitioners supporting schools in low-SES contexts, our results suggest that brief online training in behaviours teachers already feel confident about is unlikely, on its own, to change student engagement. S2.

text.text: With three first-order factors, a higherorder model is statistically equivalent to the correlated-factor model, so these results are consistent with treating engagement as a multidimensional construct with a common core [S1,S2], which is how we scored it (the mean of the three subscales).

The behavioural subscale's reverse-keyed item ('I did just enough to get by') loaded weakly and negatively even after reverse-scoring (standardised loading -0.09 in mathematics and -0.18 in PE), so many students seem to have read it as a positive statement; this explains that subscale's low alpha (Supplementary Table S3).

The four-factor and higher-order models fitted similarly (mathematics CFI 0.95 and 0.94; PE CFI 0.96 and 0.96), and both fitted far better than a single factor, with or without variety.
